      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Head</span> and Neck Cancer</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer? <p><span class="qt0">Head</span> and neck cancer is the name for cancers that develop in the mouth, nose and sinuses, salivary glands, and throat and voice box (larynx). Most <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancers are squamous cell cancers. They begin in the moist tissues that line the <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck. The cancer cells may spread into deeper tissue as the cancer grows.</p><p>There are other cancers that develop in the <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck, such as brain cancer, eye cancer, and esophageal cancer. But they are usually not considered to be <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancers, because those types of cancer and their treatments are different.</p>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer? <p>Anyone can get <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer, but you are more likely to develop it if you:</p><ul><li>Use tobacco or drink lots of alcohol. Your risk of developing <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer is even higher if you do both.</li><li>Are male.</li><li>Are over age 50.</li><li>Have a history of <span class="qt0">head</span> or neck cancer.</li><li>Have HPV (for cancers in the tonsils and base of the tongue).</li><li>Are exposed to wood dusts or certain other toxic substances at work (for upper throat, nose, and sinus cancers).</li><li>Have had radiation exposure to the <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck (for salivary gland cancer).</li><li>Have Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (for upper throat and salivary gland cancers).</li><li>Are Asian (for upper throat cancer).</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer?<p>The symptoms of <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer may include:</p><ul><li>A lump in the neck</li><li>A sore in the mouth or the throat that does not heal and may be painful</li><li>A sore throat that does not go away</li><li>Trouble swallowing</li><li>A change or hoarseness in the voice</li></ul><p>Other possible symptoms can depend on the specific type of <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer.</p>How is <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer diagnosed?<p>Which exams and tests used to diagnose <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer can depend on the specific type of cancer. Possible exams and tests may include:</p><ul><li>A physical exam of the area that might have cancer.</li><li>Blood and/or urine tests.</li><li>An endoscopy.</li><li>A biopsy or other procedure to collect cells from the area that might have cancer. The cells are viewed under a microscope to find out if they are abnormal.</li><li>Imaging tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer?<p>The treatment for <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer will depend on the specific type of cancer, the stage (how advanced the cancer is), your overall health, and other factors. The treatment options might include:</p><ul><li>Surgery</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Cancer immunotherapy</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that mainly attack specific cancer cells and cause less harm to normal cells</li></ul><p>In some cases, you may need a combination of treatments. Sometimes surgery can affect how well you can chew, swallow, or talk. Rehabilitation, such as physical therapy, dietary counseling, and speech therapy, may help.</p>Can <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to help prevent <span class="qt0">head</span> and neck cancer:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol use or not drinking at all</li><li>Getting regular dental exams</li><li>Talking to your provider about HPV vaccination</li></ul><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/headinjuries.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Head</span> Injuries</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cranial Injuries</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Skull Fractures</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Skull Injuries</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Chances are you've bumped your <span class="qt0">head</span> before.  Often, the injury is minor because your skull is hard and it protects your brain.  But other <span class="qt0">head</span> injuries can be more severe, such as a skull fracture, concussion, or traumatic brain injury.</p><p><span class="qt0">Head</span> injuries can be open or closed.  A closed injury does not break through the skull.  With an open, or penetrating, injury, an object pierces the skull and enters the brain.  Closed injuries are not always less severe than open injuries.</p><p>Some common causes of <span class="qt0">head</span> injuries are falls, motor vehicle accidents, violence, and sports injuries.</p><p>It is important to know the warning signs of a moderate or severe <span class="qt0">head</span> injury.  Get help immediately if the injured person has:</p><ul><li>A <span class="qt0">headache</span> that gets worse or does not go away</li><li>Repeated vomiting or nausea</li><li>Convulsions or seizures</li><li>An inability to wake up</li><li>Dilated (enlarged) pupil in one or both eyes</li><li>Slurred speech</li><li>Weakness or numbness in the arms or legs</li><li>Loss of coordination</li><li>Increased confusion, restlessness, or agitation</li></ul><p>Doctors use a neurologic exam and imaging tests to make a diagnosis. Treatment depends on the type of injury and how severe it is.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/headlice.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Head</span> Lice</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Pediculosis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are <span class="qt0">head</span> lice?<p><span class="qt0">Head</span> lice are tiny insects that live on people's <span class="qt0">heads</span>. Adult lice are about the size of sesame seeds. The eggs, called nits, are even smaller - about the size of a dandruff flake. Lice and nits are found on or near the scalp, most often at the neckline and behind the ears.</p><p><span class="qt0">Head</span> lice are parasites, and they need to feed on human blood to survive. They are one of the three types of lice that live on humans. The other two types are body lice and pubic lice. Each type of lice is different, and getting one type does not mean that you will get another type.</p>How do <span class="qt0">head</span> lice spread?<p>Lice move by crawling, because they cannot hop or fly. They spread by close person-to-person contact. Rarely, they can spread through sharing personal belongings such as hats or hairbrushes. Personal hygiene and cleanliness have nothing to do with getting <span class="qt0">head</span> lice. You also cannot get pubic lice from animals. <span class="qt0">Head</span> lice do not spread disease.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt0">head</span> lice?<p>Children ages 3-11 and their families get <span class="qt0">head</span> lice most often. This is because young children often have <span class="qt0">head-to-head</span> contact while playing together.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">head</span> lice?<p>The symptoms of <span class="qt0">head</span> lice include:</p><ul><li>Tickling feeling in the hair</li><li>Frequent itching, which is caused by an allergic reaction to the bites</li><li>Sores from scratching. Sometimes the sores can become infected with bacteria.</li><li>Trouble sleeping, because <span class="qt0">head</span> lice are most active in the dark</li></ul>How do you know if you have <span class="qt0">head</span> lice?<p>A diagnosis of <span class="qt0">head</span> lice usually comes from seeing a louse or nit. Because they are very small and move quickly, you may need to use a magnifying lens and a fine-toothed comb to find lice or nits.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">head</span> lice?<p>Treatments for <span class="qt0">head</span> lice include both over-the-counter and prescription shampoos, creams, and lotions. If you want to use an over-the-counter treatment and you aren't sure which one to use or how to use one, ask your health care provider or pharmacist. You should also check with your health care provider first if you are pregnant or nursing, or if you want to use a treatment on a young child.</p><p>Follow these steps when using a <span class="qt0">head</span> lice treatment:</p><ul><li>Apply the product according to the instructions. Only apply it to the scalp and the hair attached to the scalp. You should not use it on other body hair.</li><li>Use only one product at a time, unless your health care provider tells you to use two different kinds at once</li><li>Pay attention to what the instructions say about how long you should leave the medicine on the hair and on how you should rinse it out</li><li>After rinsing, use a fine-toothed comb or special "nit comb" to remove dead lice and nits</li><li>After each treatment, check your hair for lice and nits.  You should comb your hair to remove nits and lice every 2-3 days. Do this for 2-3 weeks to be sure that all lice and nits are gone.</li></ul><p>All household members and other close contacts should be checked and treated if necessary. If an over-the-counter treatment does not work for you, you can ask your health care provider for a prescription product.</p>Can <span class="qt0">head</span> lice be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to prevent the spread of lice. If you already have lice, besides treatment, you should:</p><ul><li>Wash your clothes, bedding, and towels with hot water, and dry them using the hot cycle of the dryer</li><li>Soak your combs and brushes in hot water for 5-10 minutes</li><li>Vacuum the floor and furniture, particularly where you sat or lay</li><li>If there are items that you cannot wash, seal them in a plastic bag for two weeks</li></ul><p>To prevent your children from spreading lice:</p><ul><li>Teach children to avoid <span class="qt0">head-to-head</span> contact during play and other activities</li><li>Teach children not to share clothing and other items that they put on their <span class="qt0">head</span>, such as headphones, hair ties, and helmets</li><li>If your child has lice, be sure to check the policies at school and/or daycare. Your child may not be able to go back until the lice have been completely treated.</li></ul><p>There is no clear scientific evidence that lice can be suffocated by home remedies, such as mayonnaise, olive oil, or similar substances. You also should not use kerosene or gasoline; they are dangerous and flammable.</p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention </p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/concussion.html">
      <content name="title">Concussion</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Brain Concussion</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Brain Injury</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A concussion is a type of brain injury.  It involves a short loss of normal brain function. It happens when a hit to the <span class="qt0">head</span> or body causes your <span class="qt0">head</span> and brain to move rapidly back and forth. This sudden movement can cause the brain to bounce around or twist in the skull, creating chemical changes in your brain. Sometimes it can also stretch and damage your brain cells.</p><p>Sometimes people call a concussion a "mild" brain injury. It is important to understand that while concussions may not be life-threatening, they can still be serious.</p><p>Concussions are a common type of sports injury. Other causes of concussions include blows to the <span class="qt0">head</span>, bumping your <span class="qt0">head</span> when you fall, being violently shaken, and car accidents.</p><p>Symptoms of a concussion may not start right away; they may start days or weeks after the injury. Symptoms may include a <span class="qt0">headache</span> or neck pain. You may also have nausea, ringing in your ears, dizziness, or tiredness. You may feel dazed or not your normal self for several days or weeks after the injury. Consult your health care professional if any of your symptoms get worse, or if you have more serious symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>Convulsions or seizures</li><li>Drowsiness or inability to wake up</li><li>A <span class="qt0">headache</span> that gets worse and does not go away</li><li>Weakness, numbness, or decreased coordination</li><li>Repeated vomiting or nausea</li><li>Confusion</li><li>Slurred speech</li><li>Loss of consciousness</li></ul><p>To diagnose a concussion, your health care provider will do a physical exam and will ask about your injury. You will most likely have a neurological exam, which checks your vision, balance, coordination, and reflexes. Your health care provider may also evaluate your memory and thinking. In some cases, you may also have a scan of the brain, such as a CT scan or an MRI. A scan can check for bleeding or inflammation in the brain, as well as a skull fracture (break in the skull).</p><p>Most people recover fully after a concussion, but it can take some time. Rest is very important after a concussion because it helps the brain to heal. In the very beginning, you may need to limit physical activities or activities that involve a lot of concentration, such as studying, working on the computer, or playing video games. Doing these may cause concussion symptoms (such as <span class="qt0">headache</span> or tiredness) to come back or get worse. Then when your health care provider says that it is ok, you can start to return to your normal activities slowly.</p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/traumaticbraininjury.html">
      <content name="title">Traumatic Brain Injury</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">TBI</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Acquired brain injury</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is traumatic brain injury (TBI)?<p>Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a sudden injury that causes damage to the brain. It may happen when there is a blow, bump, or jolt to the <span class="qt0">head</span>. This is a closed <span class="qt0">head</span> injury. A TBI can also happen when an object penetrates the skull. This is a penetrating injury.</p><p>Symptoms of a TBI can be mild, moderate, or severe. Concussions are a type of mild TBI. The effects of a concussion can sometimes be serious, but most people completely recover in time. More severe TBI can lead to serious physical and psychological symptoms, coma, and even death.</p>What causes traumatic brain injury (TBI)?<p>The main causes of TBI depend on the type of <span class="qt0">head</span> injury:</p><ul><li>Some of the common causes of a closed <span class="qt0">head</span> injury include 
	<ul><li>Falls. This is the most common cause in adults age 65 and older.</li><li>Motor vehicle crashes. This is the most common cause in young adults.</li><li>Sports injuries</li><li>Being struck by an object</li><li>Child abuse. This is the most common cause in children under age 4.</li><li>Blast injuries due to explosions</li></ul>
</li><li>Some of the common causes of a penetrating injury include 
	<ul><li>Being hit by a bullet or shrapnel</li><li>Being hit by a weapon such as a hammer, knife, or baseball bat</li><li>A <span class="qt0">head</span> injury that causes a bone fragment to penetrate the skull</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Some accidents such as explosions, natural disasters, or other extreme events can cause both closed and penetrating TBI in the same person.</p>Who is at risk for traumatic brain injury (TBI)?<p>Certain groups are at higher risk of TBI:</p><ul><li>Men are more likely to get a TBI than women. They are also more likely to have serious TBI.</li><li>Adults aged 65 and older are at the greatest risk for being hospitalized and dying from a TBI</li></ul>What are the symptoms of traumatic brain injury (TBI)?<p>The symptoms of TBI depend on the type of injury and how serious the brain damage is.</p><p>The symptoms of mild TBI can include:</p><ul><li>A brief loss of consciousness in some cases. However, many people with mild TBI remain conscious after the injury.</li><li><span class="qt0">Headache</span></li><li>Confusion</li><li>Lightheadedness</li><li>Dizziness</li><li>Blurred vision or tired eyes</li><li>Ringing in the ears</li><li>Bad taste in the mouth</li><li>Fatigue or lethargy</li><li>A change in sleep patterns</li><li>Behavioral or mood changes</li><li>Trouble with memory, concentration, attention, or thinking</li></ul><p>If you have a moderate or severe TBI, you may have those same symptoms. You may also have other symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>A <span class="qt0">headache</span> that gets worse or does not go away</li><li>Repeated vomiting or nausea</li><li>Convulsions or seizures</li><li>Not being able to wake up from sleep</li><li>Larger than normal pupil (dark center) of one or both eyes. This is called dilation of the pupil.</li><li>Slurred speech</li><li>Weakness or numbness in the arms and legs</li><li>Loss of coordination</li><li>Increased confusion, restlessness, or agitation</li></ul>How is traumatic brain injury (TBI) diagnosed?<p>If you have a <span class="qt0">head</span> injury or other trauma that may have caused a TBI, you need to get medical care as soon as possible. To make a diagnosis, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your symptoms and the details of your injury</li><li>Will do a neurologic exam</li><li>May do imaging tests, such as a CT scan or MRI</li><li>May use a tool such as the Glasgow coma scale to determine how severe the TBI is. This scale measures your ability to open your eyes, speak, and move.</li><li>May do neuropsychological tests to check how your brain is functioning</li></ul>What are the treatments for traumatic brain injury (TBI)?<p>The treatments for TBI depend on many factors, including the size, severity, and location of the brain injury.</p><p>For mild TBI, the main treatment is rest. If you have a <span class="qt0">headache</span>, you can try taking over-the-counter pain relievers. It is important to follow your health care provider's instructions for complete rest and a gradual return to your normal activities. If you start doing too much too soon, it may take longer to recover. Contact your provider if your symptoms are not getting better or if you have new symptoms.</p><p>For moderate to severe TBI, the first thing health care providers will do is stabilize you to prevent further injury. They will manage your blood pressure, check the pressure inside your skull, and make sure that there is enough blood and oxygen getting to your brain.</p><p>Once you are stable, the treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Surgery to reduce additional damage to your brain, for example to
	<ul><li>Remove hematomas (clotted blood)</li><li>Get rid of damaged or dead brain tissue</li><li>Repair skull fractures</li><li>Relieve pressure in the skull</li></ul>
</li><li>Medicines to treat the symptoms of TBI and to lower some of the risks associated with it, such as
	<ul><li>Anti-anxiety medication to lessen feelings of nervousness and fear</li><li>Anticoagulants to prevent blood clots</li><li>Anticonvulsants to prevent seizures</li><li>Antidepressants to treat symptoms of depression and mood instability</li><li>Muscle relaxants to reduce muscle spasms</li><li>Stimulants to increase alertness and attention</li></ul>
</li><li>Rehabilitation therapies, which can include therapies for physical, emotional, and cognitive difficulties:
	<ul><li>Physical therapy, to build physical strength, coordination, and flexibility</li><li>Occupational therapy, to help you learn or relearn how to perform daily tasks, such as getting dressed, cooking, and bathing</li><li>Speech therapy, to help you to with speech and other communication skills and treat swallowing disorders</li><li>Psychological counseling, to help you learn coping skills, work on relationships, and improve your emotional well-being</li><li>Vocational counseling, which focuses on your ability to return to work and deal with workplace challenges</li><li>Cognitive therapy, to improve your memory, attention, perception, learning, planning, and judgment</li></ul></li></ul><p>Some people with TBI may have permanent disabilities. A TBI can also put you at risk for other health problems such as anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Treating these problems can improve your quality of life.</p>Can traumatic brain injury (TBI) be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to prevent <span class="qt0">head</span> injuries and TBIs:</p><ul><li>Always wear your seatbelt and use car seats and booster seats for children</li><li>Never drive under the influence of drugs or alcohol</li><li>Wear a properly fitting helmet when riding a bicycle, skateboarding, and playing sports like hockey and football</li><li>Prevent falls by
	<ul><li>Making your house safer. For example, you can install railings on the stairs and grab bars in the tub, get rid of tripping hazards, and use window guards and stair safety gates for young children.</li><li>Improving your balance and strength with regular physical activity</li></ul>
</li></ul></content>
